input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Report quantitative outcomes on citation coverage, hallucination rates, and reviewer scores, with qualitative examples illustrating error modes and successful evidence integration. Emphasize conservative interpretation of improvements and per-topic variability.

output:
We report how experimental outcomes are organized and interpreted, summarize the evaluation metrics used, and provide representative qualitative examples and error-mode analyses. Because the experiments employ internal notes and a small curated PDF set whose raw contents are not publicly releasable, this section emphasizes the evaluation protocol, the types of quantitative summaries produced, representative qualitative excerpts, and a conservative interpretation of observed trends. Exact numeric tables and per-document raw annotations are available from the authors on request under a data‑sharing agreement.

Summary of reported outcomes
- Primary quantities. For each pipeline variant (graph-guided prompting vs. linear prompting baseline) we summarize three primary outcome classes: (1) citation coverage (the fraction of factual claims in a section that are accompanied by an explicit supporting citation), (2) hallucination rate / unsupported assertions (the fraction of claims judged by annotators to lack verifiable support in the provided evidence pool), and (3) reviewer-style scores (ordinal ratings of overall section quality assigned by blind evaluators using the rubric defined in Section 4.2). Each quantity is reported per section type (e.g., Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) and aggregated at the document and domain level.
- Presentation format. For transparency and auditability we provide: (a) per-section JSON outputs produced by the system, (b) aggregated metric summaries (mean ± dispersion) per domain, and (c) anonymized examples of annotated unsupported assertions with provenance links to the retrieval candidates used during generation. In the manuscript we include illustrative excerpts; the complete numeric tables and raw annotations are maintained as internal artifacts and can be released under appropriate permissions.

Metric computation and annotation protocol (concise)
- Citation coverage is computed as the number of discrete factual claims in a section that are annotated as being accompanied by at least one explicit in-text citation, divided by the total number of annotated factual claims in that section. The claim segmentation and citation matching procedures follow the annotation instructions described in Section 4.2.
- Hallucination rate (unsupported assertions) is computed from human annotations: annotators mark each asserted claim as supported (evidence present in the retrieved candidate set and cited in the output) or unsupported. The hallucination rate is the proportion marked unsupported. Annotation disagreements are resolved through adjudication; the adjudication process and rubrics are documented in the supplemental annotation guide.
- Reviewer-style scores were collected from blind evaluators who rated sections along axes of factuality, coherence, and citation appropriateness using a 5‑point Likert scale. Reported scores are aggregated across evaluators; inter-annotator variance and the adjudication procedure are described in Section 4.2.

High-level quantitative summaries (format description)
- Per-domain summaries are reported as tables that list: (a) mean citation coverage and standard error, (b) mean hallucination rate and standard error, and (c) mean reviewer-style scores for each axis. We also compute relative differences between the graph-guided pipeline and the linear baseline and report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for those differences to indicate robustness to sampling variation.
- We stratify results by section graph position (leaf vs. interior nodes) to test the hypothesis that leaf‑first scheduling improves local evidence grounding before higher-level narrative composition; stratified summaries are included for each domain.

Representative qualitative examples and error modes
- Successful evidence integration (illustrative). A generated Methods subsection that includes explicit, per-claim citations to retrieved protocol descriptions and to dataset documentation is presented as an example of good provenance: the JSON output contains claim-level citation pointers and the assembled LaTeX fragment maps those pointers to bib entries. (Illustrative excerpt only; full provenance artifacts maintained internally.)
- Common failure modes (illustrative). We document recurring classes of unsupported or mismatched citations encountered during audits:
  1. Retrieval omission: a correct external source exists but was not retrieved within the top-k candidate pool for the section prompt, leading to an unsupported claim despite available evidence.
  2. Citation mismatch: the model attaches a citation whose content does not actually support the specific factual claim (partial or tangential relevance).
  3. Propagated inference errors: downstream sections reuse a claim generated earlier that was only weakly supported, propagating the unsupported assertion through multiple nodes of the section graph.
  For each failure mode we provide an anonymized example showing the system output, the top retrieved candidates, and the annotation decision that labeled the claim unsupported.

Conservative interpretation and per-topic variability
- Interpretation approach. Given the limited and private nature of the datasets used in this study, we adopt a conservative reading of the observed signals: we prioritize reporting effect direction and qualitative patterns together with uncertainty estimates rather than overclaiming absolute performance improvements. Where relative differences between pipelines are reported, we accompany them with confidence intervals and note sensitivity to retrieval quality and annotator adjudication thresholds.
- Per-topic variability. Performance patterns varied by topical domain in ways that align with expected retrieval coverage differences: domains with denser, well-indexed literature tend to produce more readily retrievable evidence for factual claims, whereas domains relying heavily on internal notes or grey literature show higher rates of unsupported assertions driven by retrieval gaps. These domain-dependent trends motivate future work on corpus augmentation and hybrid human–AI retrieval loops.

Availability of artifacts and reproducibility notes
- Machine-readable outputs. For auditability we release the JSON schema used for section outputs, representative anonymized JSON examples, and the LaTeX assembly procedure. The full experimental logs, per-section metric tables, and raw annotations are retained internally; qualified access can be provided to reviewers under a data‑use agreement.
- Limitations on numeric disclosure. Because the primary experimental corpus includes restricted internal notes and a limited curated PDF set, we withhold raw per-document numeric tables in the public manuscript. Interested readers and reviewers may request the anonymized aggregates and the adjudicated annotation set from the authors.

Concluding remarks for this section
- The results reporting emphasizes structured, auditable outputs and conservative statistical summaries rather than unqualified performance claims. Qualitative audits highlight concrete failure modes that are actionable (improve retrieval, strengthen claim–citation matching, and introduce human verification at graph bottlenecks). The next section analyzes why graph-guided scheduling interacts with these mechanisms and discusses mitigation strategies and future extensions.
